summary: SDP has a capability negotiation framework, already extended for media capabilities. This memo extends it further so endpoints can negotiate miscellaneous capabilities within the usual SDP offer/answer procedures.

eli5.summary: Two callers list what extras they can do before the call and agree on a set that both can handle.

questions: what are bcap ccap and icap in sdp
how to offer pstn and ip in sdp
subtitle: Lets two endpoints offer alternative bandwidth, connection address and title settings inside SDP capability negotiation.

tldr.problem: SDP capability negotiation could already offer alternative transports, attributes and media formats, but not alternative bandwidth (b=), connection data (c=) or title (i=) lines.
tldr.mechanism: Three new capability attributes, bcap, ccap and icap, carry numbered alternatives that potential, latent and actual configurations can reference, each with its own option tag.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can now offer, for example, an IP bearer or a PSTN circuit-switched bearer, or alternative titles such as English and Spanish, within the normal offer/answer exchange.

today: RFC 7006 is a Proposed Standard (September 2013). The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Extend SDP Capability Negotiation
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions. The SDP Capability Negotiation framework (RFC 5939) lets endpoints negotiate capabilities such as support for RTP and SRTP, and RFC 6871 adds media capabilities. All of this is embedded in the SDP offer/answer procedure of RFC 3264.

RFC 7006 adds three more things that can be negotiated: bandwidth (the b= line), connection data (the c= line) and session or media titles (the i= line). Because the three are independent, the RFC does not expect every implementation to support all of them, so each has a self-contained section and its own option tag.
sections.eli5: SDP already let callers trade lists of what they can do. This memo adds three more things to the list: how much bandwidth, where to connect, and what to call the stream.

sections.title: Capability Attributes and Configurations
sections.content:
Each new capability is an SDP attribute: bcap for bandwidth, ccap for connection data and icap for titles. They use only the att-field:att-value form. Every capability carries a number that must be unique among capabilities of the same type in the whole session description, between 1 and 2^31-1.

The capabilities are then referenced from configuration attributes: potential configurations (a=pcfg), latent configurations (a=lcfg) and actual configurations (a=acfg). In a pcfg or lcfg the references look like b=1, c=1 or i=1. An optional + in front marks the extension as mandatory, so an endpoint that does not support it must treat that potential configuration as not valid.

The capability attributes may appear at session level or media level. A capability declared at session level is interpreted as session level in the resulting SDP, and one declared at media level is interpreted as media level.
sections.eli5: Each extra gets a number tag, like numbered seats. A later line says which numbered seats to use, and a plus sign means the other side must understand it.

sections.title: The Bandwidth Capability (bcap)
sections.content:
SDP's b=<bwtype>:<bandwidth> line gives the proposed bandwidth for a session or media stream. The bcap attribute lists such bandwidths as capabilities: a=bcap:<number> <bwtype>:<bandwidth>. The RFC notes this is useful when negotiating media encodings that need different bandwidths.

In a potential or latent configuration, a bandwidth parameter is written b= followed by a comma-separated list of capability numbers, with alternatives separated by a vertical bar. The RFC allows several b= lines per configuration, even for the same bandwidth type, because SDP does not forbid that either. In an actual configuration the parameter is b= plus the list of selected numbers.

The option tag is bcap-v0. Endpoints using bcap SHOULD add it to the tags in their csup and creq attributes.
sections.eli5: It lets each side say how much of the pipe it wants to use, and offer several amounts to choose from.

sections.title: The Connection Data Capability (ccap)
sections.content:
The c= line says where media should be sent: a network type, an address type and a connection address. The ccap attribute offers alternatives as a=ccap:<number> <nettype> <addrtype> <connection-address>. The main use case is offering a choice between an IP bearer (IN) and a circuit-switched bearer (PSTN).

There is one important limit. The Standards Track way to negotiate alternative IP addresses is ICE (RFC 5245), and ccap does not change that. The combined actual and potential configurations for a media description MUST NOT use ccap to negotiate more than one address with the IN network type, so it cannot select between IPv4 and IPv6 or between different IP addresses.

The RFC does not define any way to negotiate port numbers, so the port from the m= line MUST be used by default. The exception it defines is network type PSTN, where the port is replaced with 9, the discard port. An endpoint offering both bearers MUST put the IP media description in the actual configuration and the PSTN one in the potential configuration.

Each alternative in a configuration holds only one connection capability number, since a media block permits only one c= line. The option tag is ccap-v0.
sections.eli5: It is like saying you can be reached on the internet, or on an old-style phone line. You can offer both, but you cannot offer two different internet addresses this way.

sections.title: The Title Capability (icap)
sections.content:
The i= line holds human-readable text about a session or a media stream. The icap attribute offers alternative texts: a=icap:<number> <text>, for instance a=icap:1 Document Camera. The RFC's motivating cases are an audio stream offered in English or Spanish, or a video stream offered from a speaker camera, a group camera or a document viewer. The title helps the answering user choose, and the machine-readable a=label attribute tells the offerer what was chosen.

The icap attribute itself is not subject to a=charset, because that would stop alternatives from using different character sets. Instead, the title is interpreted using the charset value of the configuration that includes it. The RFC's example pairs two titles with a=acap lines that set ISO-8859-1 and UTF-8.

Each alternative holds a single title number. The option tag is icap-v0. The RFC expects it to typically appear in csup and rarely in creq, since ignoring a title usually still leaves a usable configuration.
sections.eli5: It lets you give the same stream different name tags, like an English label and a Spanish label, so the other person can pick the one that makes sense to them.

sections.title: Offer/Answer Behavior and Field Replacement
sections.content:
To use the extension, the offerer defines capability values following the normal rules for b=, c= and i= lines, MUST include them in the offer, and references them from pcfg attributes after the media line (bandwidth and title capabilities may also be referenced from lcfg). The offer SHOULD list the needed extension level in a creq attribute.

The answerer SHOULD pick the most preferred configuration it can support for each media stream, as RFC 5939 describes. If the chosen configuration uses a connection data capability, it uses the port from the offer's m= line, or 9 for PSTN. The offerer then processes the answer normally and uses the acfg attribute to verify the configuration chosen. Later changes to the session follow ordinary offer/answer rules.

To keep the media description usable by endpoints that know nothing of capability negotiation, a configuration that invokes an i= or c= line MUST replace the corresponding line in the media description. An invoked b= line MUST replace any b= of the same bandwidth type at media level, but not at session level.
sections.eli5: One side offers a menu with a favorite choice, the other picks what it can do, and the chosen items replace the plain defaults on the page.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of SDP, offer/answer, RFC 5939 and RFC 6871 all apply. The RFC then lists specific risks for each new capability.

  • An attacker who changes a bandwidth value can leave the network underused (value too high) or congested (value too low).
  • Changing the alternative connection addresses could direct media streams to a chosen endpoint, a version of the well-known voice hammer attack.
  • Altering title text could provide false information and lead to a bad choice of media streams.

If the capability values must be protected, one of the security mechanisms proposed in RFC 5939 SHOULD be used. The title is for humans only and should not be parsed programmatically.
sections.eli5: If a trickster changes the numbers or names in the offer, calls could be jammed, sent to the wrong place, or mislabeled. Locking the message helps.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the attributes bcap (Bandwidth Capability), ccap (Connection Data Capability) and icap (Title Capability) as usable at both media and session level. Only icap is subject to charset.

IANA also added the option tags bcap-v0, ccap-v0 and icap-v0, and the configuration parameter identifiers b (Bandwidth), c (Connection Data) and i (Title), which are permitted in lcfg, acfg and pcfg attributes.
sections.eli5: The official list of SDP words got three new entries, so everyone uses the same names.
